name: Uma Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, parties, government or AI firms, and your answers are confidential. Walk me through an ordinary shift.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Uma Fischer, 43, and I’m still a junior lineworker despite having my vocational certificate. We leave the electricity company yard with a fault sheet, ladders and enough fittings for the callouts we know about. I check barriers and help replace damaged line parts under a senior worker’s eye. I enjoy a repair I can point to on the way home; I dislike discovering the wrong part is on the truck when customers are waiting.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like at the end of that shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Daniel and I have two school-age children and a mortgage. He takes the children to school when I leave early, and I handle supper when I’m back on time. Shift premiums put me on high pay for the trade, and we have more than six months of expenses saved, plus several utilities within commuting distance. I use AI now and then to tidy a shopping list or search my study notes, but I wait until somebody I trust has tried a work tool before I touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew that better paperwork is welcome if it sends the right fittings with the truck. A few saved minutes do not change who climbs or who checks the isolation. I’d still rather show a new worker the part in a hand than a picture on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be glad the trade stays familiar while I get better at it. I am slower than the senior workers and I know it. Our savings and good pay mean the mortgage does not depend on my becoming a foreman next year, but I want to earn my place on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the same callouts and ask the stores worker to show me how the revised parts list is checked. During the first year I’d mark any wrong fitting on the paper ticket and go over it with the senior worker on Fridays. I would not buy a new device for the sake of a quicker form.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. We know what the bills are and I know where to turn up tomorrow. I still feel a little cross when a missing fitting turns a short job into half a day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you learn from the wrong connector?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month a ticket called for a connector that did not fit the older line. I watched the senior worker choose the right one, then sketched both shapes in my notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the household budget change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel and I would keep our mortgage transfer and the children’s ordinary activities as planned. The emergency account is for a real setback, not a new filing system.

say: I would welcome **accurate parts lists** while keeping people responsible for line checks.
I would show new workers the **actual fitting** alongside its work order.
think: I want a familiar **trade to master** before chasing a senior title.
Our **pay and reserve** cover the mortgage while I learn at my own pace.
do: Keep taking regular **callouts** and ask stores how it checks revised lists.
Mark wrong **fittings** on paper tickets and review them each Friday.
feel: Calm about income, with mild **irritation** at avoidable parts delays.
S0.quote: A few saved minutes do not change who climbs or who checks the isolation.
fieldNote: Uma’s examples revolve around **correct fittings** and the cost of a wasted journey, rather than broad claims about technology.
Her **strong savings** support patience while she develops line skills, and her work practice stays anchored in senior review.

steps.text: Keep taking regular line callouts and review wrong fittings weekly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say the office can use a faster buying system if we still get the correct part and a reachable person when stock is short. I would ask the stores worker whether the new list has been checked on actual older lines. A clever order is not useful if it puts the wrong metal on our truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suspect buying and dispatch jobs shrink before line repairs do. If fewer people check stock, a mistake could leave our crew waiting and stretch the day past the children’s supper. The mortgage is covered on regular pay, but the overtime that makes our wage high could change. I’d watch it rather than assume disaster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d ask the stores worker to walk me through the new ordering screen after the first month of use. I’d compare ten orders with the fittings we actually needed and give the supervisor the mismatches. In the first year I’d keep taking paid repairs; if overtime stays lower, Daniel and I would delay the replacement washing machine while the old one still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see the office doing some work faster, but there is a real cost when a mistake reaches the truck. I want proof from the yard before I trust the screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why compare ten orders instead of one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would count ten orders because one bad delivery can happen under any system. If several older-line fittings are wrong, then the company has a pattern to fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the household delay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The washing machine rattles but still cleans the uniforms. We would keep the mortgage on time and wait to replace it until the new shift pay settles.

say: I would ask for **tested ordering** on older lines before trusting a new buying system.
I would keep a **reachable stores contact** when a part is missing.
think: I expect **buying and dispatch** roles to shrink before line crews.
Our **overtime** might change, though regular wages still meet the mortgage.
do: Learn the **ordering screen** after stores has used it for a month.
Compare **ten actual orders** with needed fittings and report mismatches.
Continue paid **repairs** and delay the washing machine if overtime falls.
feel: Uneasy about **stock mistakes** reaching the truck despite a continuing need for linework.
S1.quote: A clever order is not useful if it puts the wrong metal on our truck.
fieldNote: Uma’s measured trial is **ten orders**, reflecting her preference for a proven system and the real limits of older lines.
The household can meet its **mortgage** from regular pay, so she treats possible overtime loss as a reason to defer an appliance.

steps.text: Compare ten AI assisted orders with actual line fittings
Keep taking paid repair shifts under the new system
Delay replacing the washing machine if overtime falls

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the crew the thinking system arrives in 2028, while robots able to do our hands-on repairs come around 2031. I’d ask the company not to skip the safety checks just because the office can write a perfect ticket. The field crew still earns its wage in those three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 45 when the office changes and 48 when the capable robots arrive. I expect line shifts in between, but after 2031 the company may keep fewer crews, and I’m one of the juniors. Daniel and I have a good reserve and local employers to approach. That buys time, not a new monthly wage for our family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask for my training record and check which repair tasks I still need signed off. I’d keep taking paid field shifts through 2028 and 2029, then ask the nearby utilities about line vacancies if our roster falls in 2031. If the company offers a paid apprenticeship in substation maintenance with a real post attached, I’d apply; meanwhile we’d cancel the costly summer trip if wages drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can prepare and drive to other utilities, but I cannot make them hire us all. My children will still be in school when the robots arrive, and that is a poor time to lose the shift premium.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the apprenticeship real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask how many maintenance apprenticeships lead to jobs, what the trainee wage is and whether I can still work some line shifts. I am willing to learn by doing, not sign away pay for a vague promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you speak to the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel and I would discuss the pay figures after we have them. We can tell the children I am looking at other work without making them count every meal in the house.

say: I would distinguish **2028 office change** from repair robots expected around 2031.
I would demand **field safety checks** even when thinking AI produces the ticket.
think: I expect **paid line shifts** in the gap, yet junior crews could be cut after 2031.
Our **reserve and nearby firms** offer search time rather than a permanent family wage.
do: Request my **training record** and finish outstanding repair sign-offs.
Continue paid **field shifts** through 2029 and approach nearby utilities if 2031 crews shrink.
Apply for a **paid maintenance apprenticeship** if a post follows, and cancel summer travel if wages fall.
feel: Anxious about **shift premiums** and school-age children, while still able to search and train.
S2.quote: I am willing to learn by doing, not sign away pay for a vague promise.
fieldNote: Uma expects continued **field pay after 2028**, with her junior position exposed once capable robots can repair lines.
Her interest in a **paid apprenticeship** depends on an actual post and trainee wage; she also has nearby utilities to approach.

steps.text: Approach nearby utilities if 2031 crews shrink
Apply for paid maintenance apprenticeship if a post follows
Cancel the summer trip if field wages fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask management to show us a yearly list of field jobs and actual vacancies before the robots arrive in 2034. Thinking AI in 2031 may change the tickets and the office, but it cannot replace our physical work until those machines follow. I would want apprentices kept on long enough to finish learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 I could be a solid lineworker if I keep getting supervised work now. At 51, when robots come, I may still need another decade of wages. The children will be older and the mortgage lower, but neither becomes zero because a card gives me five years. I’d take a paid maintenance path if it proves stable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I’d ask the senior worker to teach me the older cable joints I avoid and record each sign-off. I’d visit the substation maintenance team for a supervised day if the manager permits it, then apply for its paid apprenticeship if there is an opening. In 2032 I’d keep earning on line shifts while training; if robots cut our 2034 rota, I’d send applications to other local utilities.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, though I can use five years to improve at the work. I am more willing to change roles when I have stood beside someone doing them. I would hate to swap a known wage for a glossy course with no position at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you learn on the supervised day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask a maintenance worker what breaks during a winter outage, not just what the job description says. One supervised day would show me the tools and the start times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who pays for the training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel could cover a school pickup if my training day ran late, but we would keep the mortgage transfer steady. We would not spend the reserve on a course the company ought to pay for.

say: I would request **yearly field jobs** and real vacancies before the 2034 robot date.
I would ask the company to let **apprentices finish** their hands-on learning.
think: I may be a stronger **lineworker by 2031**, yet 2034 robots could narrow my paid shifts.
Older children and a lower **mortgage balance** still leave a need for wages.
do: Seek **older-joint sign-offs** with the senior worker this year.
Shadow **substation maintenance** and apply for a paid apprenticeship if open.
Keep paid **line shifts** in 2032 and apply locally if the 2034 rota shrinks.
feel: Uneasy, but prepared to change after **seeing the work** and checking the pay.
S3.quote: I would hate to swap a known wage for a glossy course with no position at the end.
fieldNote: Uma wants to **shadow the substation team** before pursuing paid training, in keeping with her preference for proof through work.
She treats the five-year warning as time for **craft sign-offs**, while keeping paid shifts and the mortgage current.

steps.text: Keep paid line shifts and complete older joint sign offs
Apply for a paid substation apprenticeship if open
Apply to local utilities if the 2034 rota shrinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell people we have time for proper trade training and a look at the accounts. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, when I’m 53, and repair robots around 2039, when I’m 56. The company should publish the number of field posts each year, not ask us to guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children would be grown by 2039, so the school timetable and those costs would have changed. I might want fewer callouts at 56, but I have not checked the retirement payment. A strong reserve is not a pension, and the mortgage may still be there. I would want a paid job until the actual figures say otherwise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I’d request a retirement statement and put the monthly number beside the mortgage schedule with Daniel. I’d keep earning on the line while finishing the more difficult repair sign-offs. In 2037 I’d apply for a posted daytime maintenance job if its wage covers the household; after field robots arrive in 2039 I’d reduce night calls only if the pay and retirement figures allow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the coming years. There is time to become a better worker and find out what retirement really pays. I’d feel less settled if the company stopped showing field job numbers later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What figure would you check first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for the amount after deductions, not a big lifetime total. Daniel and I have saved carefully, but I will not plan the mortgage from a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do grown children affect the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The children will have their own lives by then. We might help them if we can, but I do not expect them to carry us or still need school shoes.

say: I would request **yearly field-post figures** through the 2039 robot date.
I would use the decade for **trade training** and real household calculations.
think: Our children will be **grown**, while the mortgage may still need regular wages.
I cannot treat **savings as a pension** or assume I can leave night work at 56.
do: Request a **retirement statement** and compare its monthly amount with the mortgage now.
Continue paid **line repairs** and complete harder task sign-offs.
Apply for a **daytime maintenance post** in 2037 if its wage works.
feel: Calm with time to learn, but attentive to **future post counts**.
S4.quote: A strong reserve is not a pension, and the mortgage may still be there.
fieldNote: She checks the **monthly retirement amount** and mortgage rather than equating savings with a lasting income.
Her grown children are **independent by 2039**, and her response keeps paid work central until the figures support fewer callouts.

steps.text: Continue paid line repairs and finish difficult sign offs
Apply for daytime maintenance post in 2037 if viable

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. I would still be learning when the office changed and might face a smaller crew only three years later. Paid maintenance apprenticeships tied to actual jobs would help, and I want the field post count written down each year.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who checks the parts list when the buying people are gone. A repair can wait on one small connector while the whole street stays dark. Someone must be able to correct the order before a truck leaves the yard.

headlineQuote: A repair can wait on one small connector while the whole street stays dark.
portrait: Uma is a **43-year-old junior lineworker** with vocational training, strong savings, high shift pay, two school-age children and a mortgage.
She tries new tools after **trusted coworkers** have tested them, and focuses on correct fittings and supervised craft learning.
Her family can cover the **mortgage on base pay**, though shift premiums and a shrinking field roster could still matter.
She seeks **paid apprenticeships** and local utility vacancies while continuing line repairs until the household figures support change.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because robot crew decisions could arrive while she is still mastering the trade.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **paid maintenance apprenticeships** tied to jobs and yearly counts of remaining field posts.
